about.label: About the park
about.entityHeading: About Buddha Park (Wat Xieng Khouane Luang)
about.heading: Where the Mekong meets 200 statues
about.entityLead: Welcome to Buddha Park (Wat Xieng Khouane Luang), widely recognized as the Buddha Park of Vientiane. Located in Deua, Vientiane, Vientiane Capital, Laos, this riverside sculpture garden serves as one of the primary landmarks for travellers visiting the capital region.
about.nearbyCluster: When visiting Buddha Park (Wat Xieng Khouane Luang), visitors can easily explore surrounding historical landmarks and points of interest, including Pha That Luang and Patuxai.
about.lead: Buddha Park (Wat Xieng Khouane Luang) is a sculptural garden on the eastern bank of the Mekong, just outside Vientiane — a quiet, otherworldly place where Buddhism and Hinduism share the same lawn.
about.paragraph1: The park was founded in 1958 by Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat, a mystic priest who studied both Buddhist and Hindu teaching. He gathered local craftsmen to mould more than 200 statues in reinforced concrete, blending the two faiths into one riverside garden.
about.paragraph2: Today Buddha Park is one of Vientiane's most surreal stops. Wandering between a 40-metre reclining Buddha, a giant pumpkin you climb from Hell to Heaven, and a three-headed elephant is unlike anywhere else in Laos.
about.quote: Walk slowly — the park reveals itself one statue at a time.

history.label: History
history.entityHeading: History & Significance of Buddha Park (Wat Xieng Khouane Luang)
history.heading: From a monk's vision to a riverside park
history.intro: The story of Buddha Park is the story of one man's unusual faith — built in concrete on the banks of the Mekong.

blocks.title: Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat
blocks.text: In 1958 the mystic figure Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat founded the park. No ordinary monk, he was a shamanic recluse who blended Hinduism and Buddhism — legend says that as a young man he fell into a cave and was tutored by a Hindu hermit, setting him on a spiritual path outside orthodox religion, fusing the two faiths into one riverside garden.

blocks.title: A garden of two faiths
blocks.text: Over the following years more than 200 figures were cast in concrete — Buddhas, Avalokiteshvara, Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma, Rama and Hanuman sharing the same lawns.

blocks.title: Today
blocks.text: After decades the park remains a relaxed, slightly surreal stop on Vientiane's eastern edge, drawing travellers who cross the river from Thailand's Nong Khai.

blocks.title: A sister park across the river
blocks.text: In 1975, as Laos came under communist rule, Bunleua Sulilat crossed the Mekong to Thailand. In Nong Khai he built Sala Keoku — a sibling sculpture park born of the same vision. One river, two banks, two parks shaped by the same hand.

legend.title: The meaning of 'Xieng Khouane'
legend.text: Locals call it Wat Xieng Khouane. In Lao, Xieng means 'sacred city / city' and Khouane means 'soul / spirit', so the full name translates as 'City of Spirits'. It marks the park's identity as a 'city of statues' while hinting at the animist folk beliefs woven through it.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: The giant Pumpkin Tower (also the 'Three Realms Tower') is a three-storey sphere that mirrors the Buddhist cosmology of the 'Three Realms (Traiphum)': enter through a demon's mouth, climb narrow steps in the dark through Hell and the human world, and finally emerge into light at the top — overlooking the whole spirit-city by the Mekong, a symbol of transcending the cycle of rebirth.

folklore.title: A place of spirits
folklore.tale: In Lao folk belief the Mekong is home to spirits (Phi). Small shrines near the water ask for safety and luck — a quiet tradition elders still remember.
folklore.shrine: If you see a small shrine or offerings by the water, admire from a distance and do not disturb them.

concrete.title: Concrete Brutalist Aesthetics
concrete.text: These colossal figures were not finely carved in marble but cast on-site in industrial reinforced concrete. The raw textures and exaggerated proportions express a mid-20th-century Lao folk-art brutalism that is rough yet full of vitality — giving Buddha Park its one-of-a-kind surreal landscape.

sisterQuote.title: A mystic fate across one river
sisterQuote.text: In 1975 Luang Pu crossed the Mekong to Nong Khai, Thailand, and built the sister park Sala Keoku. One master, two parks, facing each other across the river.

faqs.q: What are the opening hours of Buddha Park?
faqs.a: The park is open daily about 08:00–17:00. Mornings are coolest and quietest.

faqs.q: How much is the entrance fee for Buddha Park Vientiane?
faqs.a: Recent visitor reports (February 2026) put the foreign-visitor entry fee at around 60,000 LAK, plus roughly 5,000 LAK if you bring a camera. Fees change — confirm the posted price at the gate.

faqs.q: How do I get to Buddha Park from central Vientiane?
faqs.a: It's about 25 km east of the centre; take a tuk-tuk or public bus toward the Friendship Bridge.

faqs.q: Is the giant pumpkin worth climbing?
faqs.a: Yes — the three-storey sphere climbs from Hell to Heaven, with a rooftop view over the Mekong.
Very — flat lawns, a riverside walk and the playful statues, but watch children on the narrow pumpkin stairs.
Buddha Park (Wat Xieng Khouane Luang) is located in Deua, Thanon Tha District, Vientiane, Vientiane Capital, Laos — about 25 km east of the city centre on the Mekong's south bank. Plus Code: WQ67+WW.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to Buddha Park take?
faqs.a: Most visitors spend 1–2 hours. Walking the lawns and climbing the three-storey pumpkin tower fits comfortably into a half-day trip from Vientiane.

faqs.q: What should I wear when visiting Buddha Park?
faqs.a: It is an active religious site: cover shoulders and knees, remove shoes where asked, and bring a hat, sunscreen and water — the concrete lawns get very hot at midday.

sculptures.label: Sculpture guide
sculptures.heading: Six figures you should not miss
sculptures.intro: More than 200 concrete figures share these lawns. These six carry the stories visitors ask about most — with the best angle for photographing each one.

items.name: The Giant Pumpkin
items.alt: Giant pumpkin-shaped tower at Buddha Park Vientiane entered through a demon's mouth
items.desc: A bulbous tower you enter through the jaws of a demon. The narrow stair climbs past scenes of hell, through the human realm, and out onto a rooftop terrace standing for heaven.
items.photoTip: Shoot upward at the demon's mouth from the base, then from the rooftop terrace for the only full-park panorama.

items.name: The Reclining Buddha
items.alt: Long reclining Buddha statue lying along the lawn at Buddha Park Vientiane
items.desc: A Buddha lying on his right side runs the length of the central lawn, one of the largest reclining figures in Laos. The calm face and long line of the body are the park's signature image.
items.photoTip: Low angle from the feet for depth; late afternoon side-light picks out the robe folds.

items.name: Three-headed Elephant (Erawan)
items.alt: Three-headed Erawan elephant statue with Indra at Buddha Park Vientiane
items.desc: The three-headed mount of Indra, covered in small carved faces. It stands for the meeting of Hindu and Buddhist imagery that defines the whole park.
items.photoTip: Stand slightly below the heads and shoot wide — the scale reads much larger than in a straight-on frame.

items.name: Shiva
items.alt: Statue of the Hindu god Shiva at Buddha Park Vientiane
items.desc: Shiva appears with the attributes of destruction and renewal, a reminder that Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat drew freely on both Hindu and Buddhist sources.
items.photoTip: Frame the upper body against open sky to keep the concrete detail clean.

items.name: Vishnu
items.alt: Statue of the Hindu god Vishnu at Buddha Park Vientiane
items.desc: Vishnu, the preserver, is shown with his traditional emblems. He balances Shiva on the same lawn — the two faiths literally side by side.
items.photoTip: Morning light from the east softens the concrete and avoids harsh shadows.

items.name: Arjuna
items.alt: Statue of the Mahabharata hero Arjuna at Buddha Park Vientiane
items.desc: Arjuna, the archer hero of the Mahabharata, is among the epic figures cast here. Scenes from the Indian epics sit alongside the Buddhist statues without hierarchy.
items.photoTip: Shoot from a low angle with the bow arm leading into the frame.

transport.label: Getting there
transport.heading: Bus 14 and every other way in
transport.intro: Buddha Park sits about 25 km east of central Vientiane on Thadeua Road, close to the Thai–Lao Friendship Bridge. Here is exactly how to get there.

bus14.title: Bus No. 14 — the classic route
steps: Start at Talat Sao (Morning Market) bus terminal in central Vientiane
Board Bus No. 14 heading out on Thadeua Road (Route 13 south)
The bus runs east past the turn-offs toward the Friendship Bridge
Ride to the final stop — Buddha Park is right by the road
Return the same way; the last buses leave in the late afternoon
bus14.tip: Fares and timetables change without notice — confirm at the terminal before you board.

items.q: Can I fly a drone at Buddha Park?
items.a: Drone rules in Laos require permission from the authorities, and parks near the Mekong and the Friendship Bridge are sensitive areas. Assume you need written permission before flying, and ask at the entrance if you are unsure.

The main lawns are flat and mostly firm, so wheelchairs and prams can reach many of the large statues. The giant pumpkin's inner stair is narrow, dark and steep, so the upper levels are not accessible.

items.q: How is Buddha Park different from Sala Keoku in Nong Khai?
items.a: Both were created by the same mystic, Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat, and both mix Hindu and Buddhist figures in concrete. Buddha Park came first in 1958 on the Lao bank; Sala Keoku followed after 1975 on the Thai bank, with taller and more elaborate structures. Many visitors see both on one cross-border trip.

items.q: Who built Buddha Park and why?
items.a: Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat, a shamanic recluse who blended Buddhist and Hindu ideas, began the park in 1958 as a way to express his vision in concrete rather than words.

stories.label: Stories & legends
stories.heading: The tales behind the statues
stories.intro: Part history, part folklore — the stories that locals and long-time guides still tell about this riverside garden.
stories.note: Legends are labelled as such; they are shared as cultural tradition rather than documented fact.

items.title: The man who built a city of spirits
items.text: Bunleua Sulilat was not an ordinary monk. A mystic and shamanic healer, he had studied under a hermit and spent years travelling before settling on this bend of the Mekong in 1958. With a handful of untrained local workers he began pouring reinforced concrete into moulds, and kept going for years.

items.title: The cave and the hermit
items.text: The best-known story says that as a young man Bunleua fell into a cave and met a Hindu hermit who taught him scripture and meditation. That encounter, the tale goes, is why the park mixes Buddhist and Hindu figures so freely — a claim repeated by guides, though no source confirms the details.

items.title: One river, two parks
items.text: After 1975 Bunleua crossed the Mekong to Nong Khai in Thailand and began again, creating Sala Keoku. The two gardens face each other across the water, built by the same hand and the same vision — a rare case of one artist's work straddling two countries.

items.title: Hell, earth and heaven in one sphere
items.text: The giant pumpkin is a textbook image of the Buddhist 'three realms'. You enter through a demon's mouth, grope up narrow dark stairs past scenes of hell and the human world, and surface at the top into daylight — a walk-through metaphor for leaving the cycle of rebirth.

items.title: Spirits of the Mekong
items.text: In Lao folk belief the river is inhabited by phi, spirits who must be treated with courtesy. Small shrines and offerings near the water ask for safe passage and good fortune — a quiet practice that long predates the sculptures.

items.title: Concrete, not marble
items.text: Nothing here was carved from fine stone. The figures were cast on site in industrial reinforced concrete by workers with no formal training — which is why the surfaces are raw and the proportions wildly exaggerated. What began as thrift became the park's signature look.

items.title: A name that means 'city of spirits'
items.text: Xieng means city, khouane means spirit or soul. Wat Xieng Khouane — the City of Spirits — describes the place exactly: a settlement of concrete beings standing where the Mekong bends.

items.title: A garden that keeps changing
items.text: Exposed to monsoon rain and tropical sun, the concrete weathers and cracks. Repair work is continuous, and some figures have been re-cast over the decades. What you see is not a finished monument but a garden still being looked after.

seasons.label: Seasonal strategy
seasons.heading: When to visit: a season-by-season plan
seasons.intro: Vientiane has three clear seasons, and each changes what a morning at the park actually feels like.
seasons.note: The table reflects the region's long-term climate patterns; individual days can differ.

rows.strategy: The best all-round window. Arrive at opening for soft light and cool air, stay on for a Mekong sunset, and expect company at the pumpkin staircase.
Visit before 10:00 or after 16:00. Carry water, rest under the trees, wear a hat — the concrete lawns radiate heat at midday.
Mornings are usually dry, so go early. The lawns turn green and the river runs high, but count on a downpour after lunch in the wettest months.

routes.label: Suggested routes
routes.heading: Routes for every kind of visitor
routes.intro: Every route starts at the main gate. Choose by how much time you have — and by who you are travelling with.

general.desc: The standard visit: the highlights, a climb, and a cold drink by the river.
steps: Enter and take the main lawn clockwise toward the three-headed elephant
Climb the giant pumpkin from the demon's mouth up to the rooftop
Walk the length of the reclining Buddha
Finish with a drink in the shade near the riverbank

general.desc: A slower read of the park, with time to sit, sketch and watch the light change.
steps: Arrive at opening and walk the lawns in the cool morning air
Study the Hindu figures — Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma and the Ramayana scenes
Break for noodles and Lao coffee at the café
Return to the riverbank for the herons and the water monitors
Stay for the late-afternoon light on the Mekong before closing

audiences.name: Families with children
audiences.focus: Flat ground, the animals, and the pumpkin — with shade breaks.
steps: Start on the flat lawns; the ground is even and easy for prams
Let children spot the animals — elephant, naga, demons and gods
Take the pumpkin slowly; the inner stair is narrow and dark
Rest on the shaded benches and keep water handy

audiences.name: Photography & nature
audiences.focus: Low sun, mist on the river, and the wildlife along the bank.
steps: Be at the gate at opening for side-lit statues and empty paths
Work the reclining Buddha from a low angle, then the elephant wide
Walk the riverbank for herons, kingfishers and water monitors
Return before closing for warm light across the Mekong

audiences.name: Low-energy & step-free
audiences.focus: Everything on the ground level, with plenty of places to sit.
steps: Follow the flat main paths — most of the park is reachable without steps
Skip the pumpkin tower; the rooftop view needs a narrow stair
Use the shaded benches between the statue groups
Plan a short 45–60 minute loop and rest at the café

facilities.label: Visitor services
facilities.heading: Facilities & nearby services
facilities.intro: What to expect in and around the park — listed by type only. We do not recommend or promote any individual business.
facilities.note: Facilities are run by different operators and may change seasonally; ask at the gate when you arrive.

items.title: Restrooms
items.desc: Public toilets are located near the entrance. Carry your own tissue and a little small change.

items.title: Parking
items.desc: Open-air parking for cars, tour vans and motorbikes sits by the gate. Shaded spaces fill early on weekends and holidays.

items.title: Food & drinks
items.desc: A small café and a few stalls serve noodles, snacks, fruit and cold drinks. Prices are modest and cash is easiest.

items.title: Places to stay
items.desc: There is no accommodation inside the park. Guesthouses and hotels are concentrated in Vientiane centre, about 25 km away.

items.title: Shops & groceries
items.desc: Small convenience stalls near the entrance sell water and basic sundries. For a full supermarket, stock up in the city first.

items.title: Fuel & charging
items.desc: Fuel stations and motorbike repair shops line the Friendship Bridge road. Charging points for electric vehicles remain rare — plan your range before driving out.

items.title: Pharmacy & medical
items.desc: Basic medicines are sold in the city; for anything serious, hospitals and clinics are in Vientiane centre.

items.title: Cash & ATMs
items.desc: Bring Lao kip in small notes for tickets, camera fees and snacks. ATMs are in Vientiane and near the Friendship Bridge, not inside the park.

items.title: Shade & rest
items.desc: Shaded benches and open lawns give you somewhere to sit down out of the midday heat.

items.title: Connectivity
items.desc: Mobile data covers most of the park. Wi-Fi, where offered at the café, can be slow.

responsibility.label: Understanding & care
responsibility.heading: What this place is — and your part in it
responsibility.intro: Buddha Park is a working religious site as well as an attraction. A little background makes the visit richer, and a little care keeps it standing.

science.title: A record of folk imagination
science.desc: The figures were designed by one mystic and built by workers with no formal art training. That makes the park a rare, unfiltered record of mid-20th-century popular religious imagination in the Mekong valley.

science.title: Concrete as a medium
science.desc: Industrial reinforced concrete was cheap and available. It allowed enormous forms at speed, but it also means the sculptures weather quickly — which is why the surface you see is partly original, partly repair.

science.title: Two traditions on one lawn
science.desc: Buddhist and Hindu figures stand side by side, along with animist spirit beliefs older than either. The park is a physical map of the religious layering that characterises Laos.

science.title: Still a place of worship
science.desc: People come to make offerings, not only to take photographs. Monks and caretakers work here; the shrines are used.

do: Dress modestly — shoulders and knees covered
Remove shoes where a sign or a local asks you to
Keep your voice low near shrines and people praying
Carry your rubbish out if bins are full
Ask before photographing people, including monks
Pay the posted fees at the gate — they fund upkeep
dont: Climb on the statues or step over the barriers
Sit on or lean against religious figures for a photo
Touch or move offerings left at shrines
Let children run uncontrolled on fragile concrete
responsibility.closing: The park has no ticket revenue from this site and receives no commission of any kind. It survives because visitors treat it with care — please help keep it that way.
